preamble: Retraction and rounding of the open vowel [a] to the open back rounded [ɒ]. In 17th-century southern English, short /a/ after /w/ was retracted and rounded to /ɒ/, merging with the vowel of lot: Middle English swan /swan/, waschen /ˈwaʃən/ and wanten /ˈwantən/ gave swan /swɒn/, wash /wɒʃ/ and want /wɒnt/. The change did not apply before velar consonants (quack, twang, wag, wax), was blocked by analogy in swam, the past tense of swim, and did not take place in Mid-Ulster English. General American later unrounded the vowel together with the rest of the LOT class (swan /swɑn/, wash /wɑʃ/).

examples.note: The rounding is conditioned by the preceding /w/. It did not apply before velars (quack, wax) and was undone by analogy in swam. Wiktionary also lists West Midland Middle English variants with /ɔ/ (/swɔn/, wonten /ˈwɔntən/).
